Beforetime
bee-FORE-time
adv.
A compound of before and time, used adverbially. Webster 1828: formerly; of old time. The Authorized Version uses it to mark what a thing used to be, usually where the change is the point of the sentence.

Biblical Definition

Beforetime marks what used to be, and Scripture uses it at hinges where something has changed for good. Its most valuable use is a parenthesis explaining an obsolete word to a later generation: Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer (1 Samuel 9:9). The inspired writer pauses to gloss his own vocabulary, which is a small but real witness to the care with which Scripture was transmitted. It marks a city’s former standing at the moment of its fall: Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword: for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms (Joshua 11:10). It marks what a man used to do before the gospel came to his city: there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one (Acts 8:9). And it marks a reputation that made a new thing astonishing: when all that knew him beforetime saw that, behold, he prophesied among the prophets… Is Saul also among the prophets? (1 Samuel 10:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BEFORETIME as formerly; of old time; in time past — a compound adverb now largely obsolete except in the Scriptures.

expand to see more

BEFORETIME, adv. — Formerly; of old time; in time past.

Used to mark a former state or practice which has since been altered.

Compounded of before, in front or previous to, and time.

Now nearly obsolete in common English, but retained in the Authorized Version.

Compare the parallel compounds heretofore, hitherto, and aforetime.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 9:9 — "(Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.)"

Joshua 11:10 — "And Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword: for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms."

Acts 8:9 — "But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one:"

1 Samuel 10:11 — "And it came to pass, when all that knew him beforetime saw that, behold, he prophesied among the prophets, then the people said one to another, What is this that is come unto the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?"

Modern Corruption

Simon of Samaria is the Bible’s case of a man who believed, was baptized, and continued to think of divine power as something purchasable, and the church has treated his name as a category ever since without much noticing how many of his instincts it has adopted.

expand to see more

Acts 8 says Simon beforetime used sorcery and gave out that he was some great one, and that the people from the least to the greatest called him the great power of God. Then Philip preached, and Simon believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip. When he saw the Spirit given through the apostles’ hands he offered money for the ability, and Peter answered, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money… thy heart is not right in the sight of God. The old trade had changed its vocabulary and kept its logic: power to be acquired, displayed, and monetised. That is worth applying honestly to any ministry organised around the transfer of anointing for a price, and it is also the origin of the word simony.

1 Samuel 9:9 is a smaller but genuinely useful text, because it shows Scripture explaining itself across a change in usage. The writer knows his readers no longer say seer, so he tells them what it meant. That is a model for how the church should handle its own vocabulary: not by abandoning the older word, which carries something the newer one has lost, but by explaining it. The whole enterprise of this dictionary rests on the same conviction, and 1 Samuel 9:9 is its warrant — an inspired gloss, placed in parentheses, so that a later generation would not lose the sense.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lephanim (H6440 with preposition), formerly, in former times; ethmol (H865), yesterday, formerly; Greek proteron (G4386), before, formerly; prouparcho (G4391), to exist previously.

expand to see more

Hebrew lephanim — literally to the face, and so before, formerly; the beforetime of 1 Samuel 9:9 and Joshua 11:10.

Hebrew ethmol (H865) — yesterday, in time past; often joined with shilshom, the day before, for the idiom of former days.

Greek proteron (G4386) — formerly, before; ye know how through infirmity of the flesh I preached the gospel unto you at the first (Galatians 4:13).

Greek prouparcho (G4391) — to be before, to exist previously; Simon, which beforetime… used sorcery (Acts 8:9).

Hebrew roeh (H7203) — a seer; the older title glossed as prophet in 1 Samuel 9:9.

Usage

"He that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer (1 Samuel 9:9) — Scripture glossing its own older vocabulary."

"Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms (Joshua 11:10) — a former standing named at the moment of its fall."

"Simon, which beforetime… used sorcery (Acts 8:9) — the old trade with a new vocabulary and the same logic."
